267.title: A leaf, a flower, a little water
267.hook: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: the road that runs on love
267.carry: bhakti: love itself is a road to God
267.tomorrow: nine ways to love God. which one is yours?
267.howItsDone: For many Hindus, bhakti is the heart of daily religious life: offering flowers, water, food or a lamp to a chosen form of God at home or in the temple, singing devotional songs, and repeating a divine name.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Last week: karma yoga, and its line, seva: serving others changes the one who serves. The birds, the butcher, the curly tail, the half-golden mongoose and the saktu, the barley flour. Today, the second of the three paths.
screen: `SEVA: SERVING OTHERS CHANGES THE ONE WHO SERVES.`

segments.voice: Somebody drives two hours for a birthday. Somebody learns a song on the guitar, badly, for a wedding. Somebody keeps a voicemail for years because of the voice on it. Nobody asked them to. It made no sense on paper. It was love, and love has its own logic. Ask Hindus what their faith is like from the inside, and some won't start with philosophy or with duty. They'll start here: with love, aimed at God. Today, bhakti.
screen: `SOMETHING RIDICULOUS FOR LOVE.` → `IT MADE NO SENSE ON PAPER.` → `LOVE, AIMED AT GOD.`

segments.voice: Bhakti comes from the Sanskrit root bhaj: to share, to take part in, to belong to, and so to love and worship. Bhakti is a sharing. You belong to God, and God, in the bhakti picture, lets you in. The Narada Bhakti Sutra, a short classic of the devotional path, begins by defining it simply: bhakti is supreme love for God. Not an idea about God. Love. In the Gita, Krishna says what that love can look like. Paraphrased: whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, that offering of love I accept. A leaf costs nothing. By that verse, a single marigold at a roadside shrine counts. The karma path asked: what do you do? The bhakti path asks: who do you love, and how? The Puranas tell of a boy who knew the answer. Prahlada was the son of a demon king, Hiranyakashipu, who hated Vishnu and wanted his son raised to hate him too. One day the king sat the boy on his lap and asked: tell me the best thing your teachers taught you. And the little boy, in his father's lap, gave the wrong answer on purpose. He listed nine ways of loving Vishnu: hearing about him, singing about him, remembering him, and six more, which open tomorrow. The king was furious. Prahlada didn't budge. That's bhakti: love itself is a road to God, open to anyone, even a child in the wrong house. It's why so many Hindu homes begin the day with something small at the shrine: a flower, a lamp, a little water.

segments.voice: Set one small thing down at a home shrine or a windowsill: a flower, a leaf, a little water, a lamp. If you pray, offer it to God as you know God and say one name, Krishna, Rama, Shiva or Devi, once, with love. If you don't, set it down for someone you love, and notice that love wants to give. A leaf is enough.
Bhakti yoga. Devotion as a path: from bhaj, to share and belong. Love for God, offered as simply as a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water.

268.title: Nine ways to love God
268.hook: nine ways to love God, and a famous name standing beside each one
268.carry: navadha bhakti: nine ways to love God
268.tomorrow: a girl wears God's garland before he does
268.howItsDone: Hindu devotional teachers often present the nine forms of bhakti from the Bhagavata Purana as a range of practices, from listening to sacred stories and singing to service and complete self-offering, and devotees tend to settle into the forms that suit them.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti yoga. A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water. And Prahlada in his father's lap, listing nine ways to love. Today, all nine.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.`

segments.voice: People love differently. Some say it. Some show it with food. Some just show up, every time, and never say a word. Some love by listening, really listening. In plenty of families the love is all there; it just comes in different shapes. Prahlada's list is the bhakti tradition noticing the same thing about loving God. It's not one feeling. It's nine doors into the same room, and tradition even gives each door a famous person who walked through it.
screen: `PEOPLE LOVE DIFFERENTLY.` → `SAY IT, SHOW IT, SHOW UP.` → `NINE DOORS, ONE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the order Prahlada gives them in the Bhagavata Purana. One: shravana, hearing the stories of God. Tradition's example is King Parikshit, who heard the whole Bhagavata before he died. Two: kirtana, singing praise aloud: the sage Shuka, who told Parikshit those stories. Three: smarana, remembering, keeping God in mind: Prahlada himself. Four: pada-sevana, serving the feet, humble, close service: the goddess Lakshmi, at Vishnu's feet. Five: archana, worship with offerings, lamp and flower and water: King Prithu. Six: vandana, bowing and praising: Akrura, who bowed to the ground when he met Krishna. Seven: dasya, being a servant: Hanuman, who wanted nothing but to serve Rama. Eight: sakhya, friendship: Arjuna, whose chariot Krishna drove into battle, as a friend. Nine: atma-nivedana, giving your whole self: King Bali, who gave everything he had, even his own head to be stepped on. Notice how the list moves: the ear, then the voice, then the mind. Then the hands, then the whole body bowing. Then relationships, servant, then friend. And it ends with a person handing over themselves. It's a ladder, and it's also a menu. Some teachers say a person may find one or two doors that fit and live there for years. A grandmother who can't sit through a sermon but sings every evening. A quiet man who never sings but sweeps the temple steps. Same room. That's the teaching, navadha bhakti: there isn't one right feeling for loving God. There are nine ways in, and the tradition honors every one.
screen: `THE EAR, THE VOICE, THE MIND.` · `THE HANDS AND THE BOWED HEAD.` · `SERVANT, THEN FRIEND.` · `GIVING YOUR WHOLE SELF.` · then, large: `NINE WAYS TO LOVE GOD.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly past the nine doors: hearing, singing, remembering, serving at the feet, offering, bowing, being a servant, friendship, giving yourself. Notice which one feels like home, not the one you think is best, and stay with it. If you pray, walk through that door now, quietly; if you don't, just notice which shape your love usually takes, with anyone.
Bhakti yoga. The nine forms of devotion, navadha bhakti: hearing, singing, remembering, serving, worship, bowing, servanthood, friendship and giving yourself.

segments.voice: Your line: navadha bhakti, nine ways to love God. Nine doors open into one room. Until tomorrow, then.

269.title: Andal's garland
269.hook: a girl tries on the garland meant for God, and a singer is carried into the temple on a priest's shoulders
269.carry: God wants the love, in any language
269.tomorrow: a hunter breaks every rule. why does Shiva stop him?
269.howItsDone: In Tamil Vishnu temples and Sri Vaishnava homes, the Alvars' hymns (the Nalayira Divya Prabandham) are sung daily, and Andal's thirty verses, the Tiruppavai, are sung before dawn through the month of Margazhi.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: navadha bhakti, nine ways to love God, nine doors into one room, from hearing to giving your whole self. Today, the singers who took bhakti into the streets.
screen: `NINE DOORS, ONE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Every December and January, in the Tamil month of Margazhi, girls and women in Tamil Nadu, and in Tamil homes far from India, wake before dawn and sing thirty short verses. A young woman wrote them about twelve hundred years ago. They call her friends to get up, bathe in the cold river, and go wake Krishna. It's a sleepover and a pilgrimage at once. Her name was Andal. She's one of twelve poet-saints called the Alvars, and the only woman among them.
screen: `MARGAZHI, BEFORE DAWN.` → `THIRTY VERSES, TWELVE CENTURIES OLD.` → `A YOUNG WOMAN NAMED ANDAL.`

segments.voice: The Alvars were Tamil poet-saints devoted to Vishnu, living roughly between the sixth and ninth centuries in the south of India. The name is usually explained as the ones immersed, drowned in God. They didn't sing in Sanskrit, the language of priests. They sang in Tamil, the language of home, and they came from every kind of background: a king, a chieftain turned highway robber turned devotee, a bard from a community kept outside the temple walls. Their songs were later gathered into the Four Thousand Divine Hymns, still sung in Vishnu temples today. Two stories. Andal, tradition says, was found as a baby under a tulsi plant by a temple priest, who raised her. Every day he wove a garland for the god, and every day she secretly put it on first and looked at herself in the well, to see if she was beautiful enough for her beloved. When the priest found out, he was horrified and made a fresh garland. That night, the story goes, the god told him in a dream: I want the one she wore. Then Tiruppan Alvar, a singer from a community not allowed into the temple at Srirangam. He'd stand by the river, lost in song. One day a priest, needing to pass, threw a stone to move him and hit him. That night, tradition says, the priest was told to carry the singer into the temple on his own shoulders. He did. That's the Alvars' gift to bhakti: God, these stories teach, wants the love first, in the language of home, from anyone.

segments.voice: Picture the edge of a room or a table where you weren't sure you belonged, and remember the singer by the river, singing anyway. If you pray, say a few words to God now in the language you think in, the way the Alvars sang in Tamil: not perfect, just yours. If not, simply rest, and let the song matter more than the wall.

270.title: Kannappa, who gave his eye
270.hook: a hunter who didn't know the rules offers Shiva everything, including his own eye
270.carry: Shiva receives love before the rules
270.tomorrow: a princess says she's already married. to Krishna.
270.howItsDone: In Tamil Shaiva temples, hymns of the Nayanars (the Tevaram and others) are sung in temple worship, images of the sixty-three saints often line the temple halls, and the Periya Puranam's stories, like Kannappa's, are retold at festivals and to children.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars, Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu, and your line, God wants the love, in any language. Andal's garland, and a singer carried in on a priest's shoulders. Today, their neighbors, the saints of Shiva.
screen: `ANDAL AND THE WORN GARLAND.`

segments.voice: A temple priest in the hills of the south arrives each morning to do the worship properly: the water, the flowers, the mantras, all in order. And every morning he finds the shrine a mess. Meat on the floor. Water splashed everywhere. Wilted wildflowers. Someone is getting in overnight and defiling it. He's heartbroken. So one night he hides, to catch whoever's doing it. What he sees, the story says, turns his idea of proper worship upside down.
screen: `A PRIEST AND HIS PERFECT RITUAL.` → `EVERY MORNING, A MESS.` → `ONE NIGHT HE HIDES.`

segments.voice: The Nayanars are the Alvars' neighbors: sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva. The poet Sekkizhar gathered their stories in the Periya Puranam, the great story. Three of them, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, left hymns, the Tevaram, still sung in Shiva temples. And one of them is the hunter the priest saw that night. His name was Thinnan. He'd found the Shiva linga in the forest and fallen completely in love. He knew none of the rules, so he worshiped the way a hunter would. He carried water in his own mouth and poured it over the linga. He brought flowers tucked in his hair. He offered the best meat from his hunt, tasted first to make sure it was good. The priest watched, horrified. Then, the story says, one of the eyes on the linga began to bleed. Thinnan didn't hesitate. He cut out his own eye and pressed it into place. The bleeding stopped. Then the other eye began to bleed. He had one eye left, and he'd need to find the spot once he was blind, so he put his foot on the linga to mark it and raised the arrow. And Shiva stopped his hand. From that day he's been called Kannappa, the one who gave his eye. The Nayanars also include a woman poet, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, whom Shiva, the story says, called mother, and a laborer, Nandanar, kept outside the temple, who longed only to see Shiva dance. That's the Nayanars' teaching: Shiva receives love before the rules. Shiva temples still keep the rituals; many teachers read the story as showing what the rituals are for.
screen: `SIXTY-THREE SAINTS OF SHIVA.` · `A HUNTER WHO KNEW NO RULES.` · `THE EYE THAT BLED.` · `KANNAPPA, WHO GAVE HIS EYE.` · then, large: `SHIVA RECEIVES LOVE BEFORE THE RULES.`

segments.voice: Think of the way you show love when nobody's grading you: clumsy, maybe too much, cooking, fixing things, showing up with the wrong flowers. See it without embarrassment, and let it be enough. If you pray, offer your own clumsy way of loving, the hunter's way, just as it is; if not, rest in it.
Bhakti yoga, through the Nayanars: sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva. Kannappa the hunter, who gave his eye, shows love that comes before the rules.

segments.voice: Rajasthan, in the days of the Rajput kingdoms. The story goes that a little girl in a royal family sees a wedding procession go by and asks her mother: who will I marry? Her mother, half joking, points to a small image of Krishna and says: him. The girl takes it completely seriously. She grows up, she's married off to a prince of a powerful royal house, and she tells everyone, calmly, that she was already married. To Krishna. Her name was Mira. Her songs are still sung today.

segments.voice: Tradition remembers Mirabai as a princess of Merta who married into the royal house of Mewar. An honest note first: very little about her is known for certain. Most of what's told comes from devotional tradition, and many songs sung in her name were likely composed later by others who loved her. But the Mira of those songs and stories is unforgettable. Her husband, tradition says, died young, and she refused to behave the way a royal widow was expected to. She sang and danced in the temple, in public, with wandering holy people, which scandalized her in-laws. Her refrain, in a song still widely sung, is roughly: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. Giridhar: the one who lifted the mountain. Gopal: the cowherd. Krishna. Then the famous story. Her in-laws, tradition says, sent her a cup of poison, disguised as holy water offered to Krishna. Mira drank it, because it came as an offering to her beloved, and it didn't harm her. Another time, a snake in a basket; when she opened it she found a garland, or an image of Krishna. Eventually she left the palace for Vrindavan, Krishna's childhood country, and then Dwarka, on the western coast, where tradition says she disappeared into Krishna's image. What Mira adds to bhakti: the love isn't only reverence. It can be the love of a bride, bold, personal, and willing to lose everything the world thinks matters. Teachers call it madhurya, the sweet love: God loved as the beloved.

segments.voice: Ask yourself what you'd keep if everything else were taken: not things, but the love you'd walk out of a palace for, a person, a faith, maybe something you've never said aloud. Let it stand plainly, without apology. If you pray, hold it up to God as Mira held up hers; if not, just let it be yours.

272.howItsDone: Across North India, families read Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas aloud and watch it performed in the autumn Ramlila, the Hanuman Chalisa is often recited on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and Surdas's songs of child Krishna are sung as bhajans, especially around Janmashtami.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mirabai, who loved God as the beloved. Mine is Giridhar Gopal. Today, two more poets of North India.
screen: `MINE IS GIRIDHAR GOPAL.`

segments.voice: The story goes that a young man named Tulsi loved his wife so much he couldn't bear a single night apart. Once, when she'd gone to visit her parents, he followed her through a storm, across a flooded river, and climbed up to her window. She was not charmed. She told him, more or less: all this passion for a body of flesh and bone. If you had half of it for Rama, you'd be free. It stung. He left, and gave the rest of his life to Rama. Whether or not it happened just like that, what he wrote next is why his name is still known.
screen: `ACROSS A FLOODED RIVER.` → `IF YOU LOVED RAMA HALF AS MUCH.` → `HE GAVE HIS LIFE TO RAMA.`

segments.voice: Tulsidas retold the Ramayana. Not in Sanskrit, but in Awadhi, a language ordinary people in the Hindi heartland actually spoke. He called it the Ramcharitmanas, the lake of the deeds of Rama. In autumn, towns and villages act it out as the Ramlila, and families read it aloud at home. The Hanuman Chalisa, a prayer to Hanuman often recited on Tuesdays and Saturdays, is traditionally credited to him too. His love is a servant's: dasya, the seventh of the nine forms. Rama is the king, and Tulsidas is his servant, happy to be. Now a very different voice. Surdas, a poet remembered by tradition as blind, sang in Braj, the language of Krishna's country, and the Krishna he saw was mostly a small child. One song sung in his name is a toddler talking to his mother. Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo. Mother, I didn't eat the butter. Then the excuses: the other boys smeared it on my face. My arms are too short to reach the pot. And Yashoda, his mother, laughing, gathers him up. That's vatsalya: a parent's love for a child, aimed at God. Here God is the kid with butter on his face, lying badly, and you're the one who loves him anyway. Two poets, two kinds of love. The servant bowing to the king. The mother catching the thief. That parent's love is why some Hindu homes care for a small image of baby Krishna like a child, even putting him to bed at night.

segments.voice: Try on two kinds of love. First the servant's: think of someone, or something, you'd gladly serve, and notice what it's like to bow a little. Then the parent's: picture a small child, one you know or the one you were, caught in a sweet, bad lie, and notice which love softens you more.
Bhakti yoga, through Tulsidas and Surdas. Tulsidas loved Rama as a servant loves a king; Surdas loved child Krishna as a mother loves a toddler caught with the butter.

273.howItsDone: Kirtan is sung in temples, homes and public processions across the Hindu world: a leader sings a line of divine names and the group answers, usually with drums (mridanga), small cymbals (kartal) and harmonium; Gaudiya Vaishnavas, including ISKCON, make chanting the name central to daily practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: God as king, God as child. Tulsidas the servant of Rama, and Surdas's toddler with butter on his face. Today, the last day of bhakti, the end of the week, and the thing you can do together.

segments.voice: Maybe you've heard it at a temple, a yoga studio, or on a city sidewalk. One voice sings a line. Everyone sings it back. Drums, little hand cymbals, sometimes a harmonium wheezing along. The same few names, over and over, a little faster each time, until people who walked in stiff and shy are swaying, eyes closed, some of them crying. It can look like a concert. It's older than that, and it's meant as a method. Today: kirtan.
screen: `ONE VOICE, THEN EVERYONE.` → `DRUMS, CYMBALS, HARMONIUM.` → `NOT A CONCERT. A METHOD.`

segments.voice: Kirtan comes from the Sanskrit kirt: to mention, to tell, to praise aloud. It's the second of the nine forms of devotion. The Alvars and Nayanars sang. Mira sang. Surdas sang. But in Bengal, Chaitanya of Nabadwip turned singing into a movement. He'd lead crowds through the streets, singing the names of Krishna, dancing, arms raised. Tradition says that when the local authorities tried to ban the public singing, he answered with an even bigger procession. For Chaitanya's followers, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, singing the divine name isn't a warm-up for devotion. It is the devotion. God, they say, is present in the name. Why does it work as a method? It's call and response, so you don't have to know anything; you just repeat. It uses the body: breath, voice, rhythm. It's done together, so the group carries your shyness. And it runs on repetition, which, people who sing it say, slowly quiets the part of the mind that keeps commentating. That's this whole week. The nine doors, one room. Andal's garland and the singer on the priest's shoulders. Kannappa's eye. Mira's cup of poison. Tulsidas the servant, Surdas's toddler. And now a whole street singing. Bhakti says the road to God can be love, all the way. Tomorrow, the third path, which asks a very different question.

segments.voice: Pick one short name or word that means something to you: if you pray, a name of God, like Rama, Krishna, Shiva or Om; if not, a word like peace, or a loved one's name. Say it softly on the out-breath, then hear it in your head as if a room answered back. Let it get slower, not faster, and let the commentary quiet.
Bhakti yoga, part seven: kirtan, singing the divine name together, call and response. For Chaitanya's followers, the name itself is the devotion.
